t: a fixed sin offering. A sin offering that always comes from an animal, unlike the 'ascending and descending' offering that varies according to a person's financial means (see Hilchot Shegagot 1:4).
even though it is not work. For example, rabbinic prohibitions (see Hilchot Shabbat 21:1 ff.).
lashes for rebellion. Rabbinic lashes.
that it is forbidden to move. Objects that the Sages forbade moving on the Sabbath (see there 24:12-13).
and anything that it is forbidden to say or do at the outset on the Sabbath. Speech and actions concerning weekday business that were forbidden on the Sabbath (see there 24:1-2).
from minchah onward. Toward evening, about two and a half hours before sunset, and onward.
the spoiled leaves. That he does not want to eat.
they may crack nuts and break up pomegranates. Crack the shells of nuts and separate the seeds of pomegranates.

because of distress. Although these actions are forbidden on the Sabbath, the Sages permitted them on Yom Kippur so that there would be no great distress at the end of Yom Kippur while waiting for food to be prepared.

and Yom Kippur that falls on the Sabbath is forbidden... all day. Because he selects the spoiled leaves from the good ones. And although even the spoiled leaves can be eaten with difficulty and so there is no Torah-level prohibition of selecting here, it is forbidden rabbinically (Maggid Mishneh).
in Shinar. Babylonia.
and in the West. The countries of northwest Africa.
another positive commandment. Besides refraining from work.
by oral tradition. According to the tradition of the Sages.
since the verse punished with karet, etc.. From the statement that one who eats is liable to karet, we learn that this act is prohibited, although it is not written explicitly.
to anoint. To rub oneself with oil for pleasure.
Sabbath with regard to work, etc.. From the word 'Sabbath' we learn the obligation to rest from work, and from the word 'Shabbaton' that there is an obligation to refrain from these pleasures.

and one is not liable to karet or an offering except for eating and drinking alone. For the Torah writes that one is punished with karet for "every soul that is not afflicted," and this verse was interpreted as referring to the prohibition of eating and drinking only (as above 1:4).
so too the rest of affliction, both by day and by night. The obligation to fast begins already from the evening, and not only in the morning of Yom Kippur (and see Hilchot Ta'aniyot 5:7).
to add from the weekday to the holy day, at its entrance and its exit. To add a little time before Yom Kippur begins and a little after it ends, during which one observes the laws of Yom Kippur.

as it says, "And you shall afflict your souls on the ninth of the month, in the evening," etc.. Although Yom Kippur is "on the tenth of the seventh month," the fast nonetheless begins already on the ninth of the month, toward evening.
"from evening to evening you shall keep your Sabbath". This implies that one must add at its exit just as at its entrance.
we do not protest against them. We do not protest against them for doing this.

so that they do not come to do it deliberately. It is very likely that they will continue in their practice, and now they are acting inadvertently, but if they find out they will be acting deliberately, which is more serious.
that are fit for a person. For human consumption. But if they are not fit for a person, he is exempt (below halachah 5).
the size of a large date. The amount of a large date.
and all foods combine. If he ate different kinds of food, all of them combine to complete the amount that makes him liable.
a mouthful. The amount of drink needed to fill the cavity of the drinker's mouth.
each one according to his own mouthful. The amount is measured for each person according to the size of his mouth, and there is no general measure for all people.
enough to push it to one side and have it look full. The amount needed to fill out a person's puffed-out cheek.
average. Whose mouth is of average size.
less than a revi'it. Less than the amount of a quarter of a log.
and eating and drinking do not combine into one measure. If he ate a little and drank a little, the food and drink do not combine to complete the amount that makes him liable.
permitted foods. For eating.
piggul and notar. Meat of offerings that became disqualified for eating (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 10:23).
and tevel. Produce from which terumot and ma'aserot have not been separated (there 10:19).
and neveilot and terefot. Animals that died or are likely to die, whose meat is forbidden to eat (there 4:1, 4:6).
and fat or blood. Which were forbidden to eat (see there 6:1, 7:1).

although it is forbidden by the Torah even at a half measure, etc.. Although the Torah prohibition of eating applies even to less than the liable amount, the punishment is only for eating the full amount.
lashes for rebellion. Rabbinic lashes.
if he ate a little, etc.. And in each act of eating there was not the liable amount.
the time it takes to eat three eggs. The time needed to eat bread in the amount of three eggs.
these combine to the full amount. Everything he ate during this time combines, and if it adds up to the full amount, he is liable.
the time it takes to drink a revi'it. The time needed to drink the amount of a quarter of a log.
foul tree saps. Liquids that flow from tree trunks, with a bad smell and taste.
brine. A sauce drawn from fish.
muries. Fish fat.
and raw vinegar. Vinegar not mixed with water, whose taste is very strong and which people do not drink that way.
but we give him lashes for rebellion. For it is forbidden in any case by rabbinic law.
vinegar mixed with water. Vinegar mixed with water, which is fit for drinking.
one who chews. One who eats, dry and raw, food that is usually eaten cooked or moist.
vine shoots. The new vine leaves at the start of their budding and growth.
that have budded. That have begun to grow.
in the Land of Israel. Where the good edible shoots commonly grow at this season.
beyond this. At a later time.

if he ate roast meat with salt, etc.. Roast meat together with salt on it. Although eating salt by itself is not considered a normal way of eating, when the salt is mixed with the meat this is its way of being eaten and it combines.

brine on top of vegetables. Vegetables with their sauce. Although the sauce is a drink, and foods and drinks do not combine together, since the sauce serves to prepare the food, it combines with it for the liable amount.

if he was full from heavy eating, so that he ate until he was disgusted with his food. He ate a very large amount until he was sick of eating more and it repels him (for example, if he ate on the eve of Yom Kippur).
and ate more than his fill. He ate more after that.

for even though this excess is fit for a hungry person, etc.. Although this food is in itself fit for another person to eat, it is considered unfit for eating for someone who has reached such a level of fullness.
who asked. Who requested.
on his own say. According to his own request and feeling alone.
until he says, "enough". And I need no more.
we feed him according to his word. The physician's.
an expert physician. One skilled in his craft.
the patient did not say he needs it, and the physicians disagree... we feed him. For this is a case of possible danger to life (see Hilchot Shabbat 2:1).
a pregnant woman who smelled. A pregnant woman who smelled food and a craving to eat it arose in her.
if her mind was cooled by this reminder. If the knowledge that it is now Yom Kippur managed to cool her craving.
we feed her. Since if she does not eat she may come to danger (see Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 5:6-8, Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 14:14).
who was seized by bulmus. An illness of a sudden attack of ravenous hunger that causes weakness of mind and dimming of the senses; if he does not eat, he is in danger.
until his eyes brighten. Until his clarity of mind returns and he sees well again.
and we do not delay him. We do not make him wait, for one must not delay where life is in danger (see Hilchot Shabbat 2:3).
we train him by hours. We train him to fast for a few hours.
at two hours. Two hours after sunrise.
according to the child's strength, we add to his affliction by hours. If the child has the strength to fast beyond this hour, he fasts.
he fasts and completes. He fasts and completes the fast of a full day, until the evening.
who have grown two hairs. Who have grown two hairs in their private area (see Hilchot Ishut 2:1, 2:10).
we do not afflict him. At all.
for thirty days. From her wedding day.
and he need not worry. There is no prohibition in this.
and a woman may rinse one hand, etc.. She washes her hand in order to feed her child with it.
even though he is not in danger. Although for eating there is no permission unless he is dangerously ill (above 2:8), for washing they were lenient.

and all who are obligated to immerse may immerse in their usual way. Anyone obligated to immerse to become pure (such as a niddah or a woman after childbirth, who are forbidden marital relations until they immerse) may immerse as he usually does.
both on the Ninth of Av. Which is also forbidden for washing (Hilchot Ta'aniyot 5:10).
nowadays. When there is no obligation to immerse for a seminal emission, and immersion does not make one fully pure, as explained below.
he wipes with a cloth. He removes the traces of the emission with a cloth, as one who is soiled with excrement does.
and he is forbidden to wash his whole body. In preparation for prayer.
or to immerse. For purification from a seminal emission.

for one who immerses nowadays is not pure of corpse impurity. He is forbidden to immerse for his purification since this immersion will not help, as he is impure with corpse impurity (unlike those obligated to immerse mentioned above in halachah 2, where the immersion does help them).
and washing after a seminal emission for prayer nowadays is only a custom. Which the people of Babylonia and Spain adopted because of "Prepare to meet your God, Israel" (see Hilchot Tefillah 4:6).
and no custom cancels, etc.. And a custom has no power to cancel the prohibition of washing.
and they did not say. In the Talmud (Yoma 88a).

but when they enacted, etc.. Initially there was a rabbinic enactment that one should not pray without immersing after a seminal emission, and afterwards it was canceled (see Hilchot Kri'at Shema 4:8, Hilchot Tefillah 4:4-5). And the law that one must immerse after a seminal emission was said only with regard to the time when this enactment was in force.
and we have already explained. Hilchot Tefillah 4:5.
mud so wet that if a person places his hand, etc.. The mud is so wet that if he touches the mud with his hand and it touches his other hand, moisture from the mud will reach it.
it is forbidden to sit on it. Since he derives pleasure from the wetness, like washing.
and cool himself with it. He may press the cold clay vessel to his body in order to cool off.
for the water seeps out of its sides. The water seeps through the walls of the vessel and wets his body.
even metal vessels are forbidden. Although the water does not seep through them.
and it is permitted to cool oneself with fruit. To cool off using cold fruits.
from the evening. In the evening.
and he places it under the garments. In order to keep it cold and moist.
and the next day he passes it over his face, etc.. He may dry himself with it, even though it is very cold and he enjoys this, and it is not considered forbidden washing.

that they not take their hands out from under the hems of their garments. That they not take their hands out from the edge of the sleeve, for then it looks as if he is washing for pleasure as he does on a weekday.
cork. The bark of the cork oak.
rushes. Reeds and soft branches.
for the hardness of the ground, etc.. Although he covers his feet with a garment, this does not prevent him from feeling the hard ground when he steps, and he is afflicted by his walking.

they prevent them from wearing a shoe or sandal. Although they are minors, wearing a sandal is not a vital need for them (unlike eating, for example), and so they did not permit them this (based on Yoma 78b).
and a woman after childbirth. A woman who has given birth.
for thirty days. After her giving birth.
to anoint. With oil and the like (Ma'aseh Roke'ach).
part of his body is like his whole body. Even anointing part of the body is forbidden.
sores. Wounds.
everywhere. Even in a place where they are accustomed not to light lamps as a rule.
for lighting a lamp on the Sabbath is an obligation. Because of Sabbath delight (Hilchot Shabbat 5:1).
